questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was looking for a place with a strong academic profile in the French language and culture, and Paris allowed me to also study and live in one of the largest cultural centers and most well-connected cities in Europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It did require some work. The information system is not too centralized - in fact the information software was not consistent between courses and a lot of information is available solely through email or given solely in person. I was not prompted with the necessary information and I had to reach out myself to a lot of different people and talk to other students to gain the information I needed to follow the courses. I did however feel that most things were easily sorted along the way.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had an international mobility coordinator, who was helpful mostly with the administrative ERASMUS-stuff, student cards and likewise. For the rest, all assistance regarding information and orientation was obtained directly from the professors, and sometimes local students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Through Sorbonne Université, the application process was fairly easy and I was offered housing in a college very quickly after submitting my application, and I had a feeling that it was quite reliable. I would recommend applying directly to Cité Universitaire, where I lived; Danish students can apply directly to the Danish house in Cité Universitaire (Fondation Danoise). The living conditions and community there were very good in my experience.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: My university, Sorbonne Université, is very well-connected with public transport, and students can get a public transport pass (Navigo) at a fair price. I don't think on campus housing was an option for me, and I found very few problems living off campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was very manual, I had to register by email to the administration, and for me it was disjoint, so different courses had different administrative personnel responsible for registration. I found the process a bit unclear, the steps are not clearly outlined, and it was tough to get confirmation of registration. However, in the end I found that I could always talk directly to the professor and things would work out.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had instructions from the international mobility coordinator, there was the administrative personnel, and the professors were very (the most) helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was registered for all the courses I wanted, so I was completely successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be on time, be patient and in the end, I felt most things were possible.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: At my host institution the Master's programme is split into two: first year of Master's (M1) and second year of Master's (M2). In my experience, M2 courses were significantly more advanced and research focused than M1 courses. Whereas M1 courses perhaps had less prerequisites than corresponding courses at my home institution (UCPH), the level was quite similar with perhaps a slightly higher pace, while the M2 courses were quite a bit more difficult in my experience than the courses I have taken in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: You had to learn a lot more of the material by heart, the focus was more theoretical and we did very little in terms of applications and implementations. There was also very little groupwork and very little creative work.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Stochastic calculus and stochastic control, Stochastic geometry and random graphs (subtitles: Scaling limits; Graphons; Random graphs), Concentration of measure and mixing times (subtitle: Concentration inequalities), Introduction to Riemann surfaces, Algebraic topology.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: In my experience, you have a lot of options and so you have a lot of freedom to choose according to your personal academic interests. Based on my own interests (all math and statistics), I was very happy with Stochastic geometry and random graphs and Introduction to Riemann surfaces because they offered introductions to topics that were unavailable to me at UCPH.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I ended up spending more on food than anticipated, but besides that I do not recall encountering any unexpected costs. There are some costs involved with buying kitchen equipment, practical stuff when moving in and then the odd fee for access to nice libraries etc here and there. Beware that you also have to pay a fee to visit the doctor in France.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Grocery items were slightly more expensive than expected, prices were as high and sometimes even a lot higher than prices in Denmark. Services (restaurants, hairdressers etc) were generally less expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were quite a lot of activities available. For example, there was a choir, there were sporting clubs ranging from standard such as running to more exotic such as fencing, and there were multiple social clubs organizing parties and open air movie nights. I ended up doing most of my extracurricular activities in the community where I lived (Cité Universitaire), since it was more practical for me.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't know, for me there are so many options in Paris, and so it is hard to give any general recommendations besides discovering the city, the museums and the parks. From sporting clubs, where you can pick up new sports and do sports with other students, to cultural events such as gastronomical, fashion and music festivals, live concerts or independent cinemas showing a curated set of classic and foreign films. You also have very good options to go outside Paris and get to experience France. But I can recommend using the options at the host institution for activities where you get to practice your French and make French friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Just experience the city, there is so much to do, even on a budget (most museums, parks and a lot of concerts are free). There are also really great libraries with a great selection of books if you are there to study.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was not too difficult, of course you have to get used to everything being organized in French and that the administrative process is disorganized so that most communication and practicalities are sorted directly with the professor. Then there are small things, for instance you are expected to make very thorough handwritten notes, and often no supplementary material is presented if you do not make it to class or if you miss something in class. A final small thing, for instance that there is a very strong culture for eating lunch in the university restaurants (Resto U, CROUS), and so there are very few other spots to hang out inside on campus (and you are not allowed to eat in other indoor spaces).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for the activities at campus, speak French fluently.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The most difficult thing to get used to was the French administration, it was at times quite disorganized and hard to figure out, but luckily it is not the main component of the experience. Another thing is that the tone is very different, you need to show a lot of respect and formality for authorities and elderly, and if you break formal conduct, you can expect to be told so and corrected quite abruptly at times. Your ability to speak French is also scrutinized in some environments.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated getting to experience the French mentality; I sometimes find that in Denmark we focus on process, whereas in France I felt a focus on just being, and even though that distinction is admittedly vague and hard to describe, I found that reflected in a lot of places - from restaurants (or brasseries) where there is little pressure to leave to activism to public transport to the abundance of parks and outdoor public spaces.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Make sure to apply for grants, Paris can be quite an expensive city to live in and there are grants available.
2. Unless you are very very good at French, I would advise signing up for a language course before/as soon as you start, because it is a good way to help you get used to using French all the time - especially for the courses.
3. Don't worry, it is going to be a great experience, and even if it can be tough to get everything organized, as long as you have housing (try to get into Cité Universitaire!!) and an Erasmus+ contract, the rest will get solved along the way.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep an eye on your email, a lot of courses are entirely organized by email. Make sure to go to the welcome event - you get otherwise hard to get practical information and meet the other exchange students with whom you share the experience.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I think the totality of it, when I got settled and everything was in full flow - that feeling of being able to make it in a new country, a new culture with new people while still having the wonder of discovering all the quirks and the marvels that you meet along the way. You can almost feel your horizon widening, your capabilities improving and your foundation getting stronger with more experiences. A specific academic thing I found rewarding was passing a very difficult oral exam in French, since that was one of the academic aims of going abroad to this destination.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language barrier, but that was also one of my main motivations for going to France, and I enjoyed this challenge very much, since French is so integral to the French experience.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
